source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Six wild-caught crows got a two-trap tube (one working trap, one decoy) that needed a tool pull. Only three of six learned to avoid the trap. Learning was slow.
numbers: Criterion 17 of 20 correct across two consecutive 10-trial blocks (binomial alpha 0.01), cap 150 trials. Three solvers (Obo, Tiga, Slevin) needed mean 103.3 +/- 20.3 trials. Three others never learned. 91.2% +/- 2.7 of all trials were pulls, not pushes.
limits: N=6, 3 solvers. Slow trial-and-error learning is also what a cue learner would show. Solvers differed from non-solvers in side-switching (22.1% vs 0%, U=9, p=0.0318).
agent_relevance: Even a 'passed' test can rest on 3 individuals and 100+ trials of practice. Do not read a first success as understanding.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfers 1 and 2 stripped the arbitrary cues (yellow discs, blue rim) one at a time. All three solvers still avoided the trap. So no single colour cue drove the choice.
numbers: Transfer pass rule: 15 of 20 correct over two blocks (alpha 0.05), or 9 of 10 in the first block. All 3 crows passed transfer 1 (blue rim kept, discs removed) and transfer 2 (discs black, rim removed).
limits: Passing both still allows several independent cue rules (for example 'away from blue rim OR toward high disc').
agent_relevance: Strip surface cues one by one (the schema's G3 idea). One removal is not enough; combinations of cues can hide.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfer 3 is the 'limit found'. The tube had two holes, only one with a base (a working trap). All three crows failed. They had avoided the hole, not the trap base.
numbers: All three crows failed transfer 3. Latency and side-switching were highest in transfer 3 for all three crows (binomial p=0.0156, n=3, chance 0.25 each). Tiga and Slevin avoided the trap on trial 1 of transfer 3, then sat at chance for the next 19 trials. Crows moved the meat between the holes without pulling it in.
quote: ...the crows had knowledge of the meat's relation with the hole as a proximate causal regularity but did not infer the existence of a distal causal mechanism (gravity).
limits: Authors note reluctance to pull food into a hole (a hole-avoidance habit) as part of the picture. N=3. 'No gravity inference' is the authors' reading, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: A solved task does not show the deep rule was learned. The learned rule was 'avoid holes', a proximate feature. Probe with a case where the proximate feature and the true cause split.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Transfer 4, the trap-table, looked different in shape, colour and material. All three solvers passed at once, choosing right on their first trial. The authors read this as analogical reasoning on a proximate cause.
numbers: 3 solvers passed trap-table. Across the four transfers the 3 crows avoided the trap on 10 of 12 first trials, but the first-trial result did not predict later trials. The 3 crows that failed the tube also failed the table. Table: wooden platform, 5 cm x 3 cm trap, 15 cm dowel tool.
limits: Only crows that learned the tube passed the table, so the transfer came from tube experience. First-trial wins alone were weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Real transfer needs a visually different task with the same structure. It is the strongest test, yet here it still only showed the shallow rule.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Causal reasoning in New Caledonian crows: ruling out spatial analogies and sampling error. Commun Integr Biol 2(4)
finding: Follow-up to rule out two alternatives. Eight new naive crows were tested on the trap-table: none passed. Also the three solvers met an inverted tube (hole on top, non-functional): they did not avoid it.
numbers: Eight naive crows, two blocks of 10 trials, none above chance (all p>0.05). Of 14 crows on the table, only the 3 tube-solvers passed. Inverted two-trap tube: all three solvers showed no end preference (all p>0.05).
limits: Same lab, same birds, so not independent. The inverted result removes the 'always avoid food in front of a hole' spatial rule, but not the 'avoid the hole' proximate rule.
agent_relevance: The inverted control is a model for a check that separates a surface rule from a causal rule: flip the cause and see if behaviour flips.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk physics for crows? Animal Behavior and Cognition 7(3):452-456
finding: Taylor's own review 11 years later. Crows attend to observable features (surface continuity, contact) but there is no evidence they reason about unobservable mechanisms (gravity, force). Yet he warns it is too early to say they cannot.
numbers: Evidence lines: trap-tube transfer 3 failure (2009); stone-dropping weight inattention (Neilands 2016); cautionary cases where a task change flipped results: apes better pulling than pushing (Mulcahy & Call 2006); crows infer weight from a breeze (Jelbert 2019); string mental simulation fail (2010) vs metatool preplanning pass (Gruber 2019).
quote: ...there does not seem to be any evidence that NC crows reason about unobservable causal mechanisms.
limits: Absence of evidence under one task format is weak. Taylor proposes a ratchet design: hidden object, then hidden agent, then hidden mechanism, in the same paradigm.
agent_relevance: Our agent: a fail on one probe format may be format, not capacity. Keep a ladder of probes of rising difficulty before concluding a limit.

source: Neilands, Jelbert, Breen, Schiestl, Taylor (2016) How insightful is 'insight'? New Caledonian crows do not attend to object weight during spontaneous stone dropping. PLoS ONE
finding: Signature test: look for an error a force-understanding animal would not make. Crows that invented stone dropping did not prefer heavy blocks. After training, the other birds clearly preferred heavy ones.
numbers: 12 crows. Only 2 invented block dropping. D4R dropped heavy 12 times and light 22 times (p=0.062). Pre-test pull: light 128 of 240 (p=0.167). After training, 11 birds chose heavy first on 125 of 140 trials (p<0.001).
quote: ...do not attend to the weight of an object when innovating stone dropping.
limits: Only 2 innovators, a lower rate than the original study. Captive-vs-wild and apparatus differences could matter.
agent_relevance: 'Insightful' success can hide a missing variable. Test whether a solver is sensitive to the variable that matters (weight), not only whether it solves.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton, Gray (2014) Using the Aesop's fable paradigm to investigate causal understanding of water displacement by New Caledonian crows. PLoS ONE 9:e92895
finding: Six crows passed four displacement tests (water vs sand, sinking vs floating, solid vs hollow, high vs low water) but failed two harder ones (tube width and a U-tube).
numbers: Water vs sand: 76.3% of drops to water (p=0.001). Sinking: 88.0%. Solid: 89.0%. High level: 86.8% (all p<0.001). Narrow vs wide: no first-drop preference (narrow first on 56% of trials, p=0.27). U-tube: 48.9% (p=0.79), at chance. Birds: 6 in Exp 1-2, 5 in Exp 3-4, 4 in Exp 5-6.
quote: ...a sophisticated, but incomplete, understanding of the causal properties of displacement
limits: Fixed task order. Authors compare to 5-7 year old children. Small N; the width fail may be motivation (either tube works).
agent_relevance: Performance is patchy: pass some causal variables, fail others of equal logical weight. Avoid grading a whole capacity from one task.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's Fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances. PLoS ONE 9:e103049
finding: A tighter redo. Three of six crows did discriminate narrow from wide tubes and switched when the water levels changed. One crow solved a coloured U-tube, but all crows failed a U-tube with the connection exposed. So the U-tube pass was a colour cue.
numbers: Narrow tube 100,224 mm3 vs wide 336,864 mm3. Three of six birds passed narrow-vs-wide equal levels and switched to wide when its level was higher. U-tube: only one crow (Kitty) passed the coloured version; all failed the uncovered one. Solid-over-hollow bias also held on a non-water platform in 3 birds.
quote: ...our results do not provide support for the hypothesis that these crows can infer the presence of a hidden causal mechanism.
limits: Reverses the width fail of Jelbert 2014 after an apparatus change (same research group). The object preference may be a bias, not insight.
agent_relevance: Changing the cue check (exposed link) revealed a shortcut. Always run a version where the arbitrary cue is removed or reversed.

source: Meta-analysis of five corvid Aesop's fable studies (Anim Cogn 2018; PMC6181768)
finding: Pooling rooks, jays and NC crows: within-task gains look like trial-and-error. Birds learn from rewarded drops, not from failed ones, and show no transfer between tasks.
numbers: N=28 birds. Water vs sand slope OR 1.04 per insertion [1.02,1.06], p<.001; float vs sink 1.05 [1.03,1.07]; hollow vs solid slope 1.01 (p=.67) but a big initial bias, intercept OR 57.02 [10.18,319.33]. After an efficient choice OR 5.00 (water/sand) and 2.43 (float/sink); after an inefficient choice not significant. Task order OR 0.81 [0.57,1.14], p=.22.
limits: Read through a fetch summary; authors not recorded. Data from five studies.
agent_relevance: Learning only from success, not from error, is also a risk for LLM retry loops. Count which outcomes actually change behaviour.

source: Kea weight-inference study (Royal Society journal, 2024; PMC11537761), replicating the Jelbert 2019 breeze task in kea
finding: A close replication in kea (parrots) failed. Kea did not use the sight of objects moving in a fan breeze to infer weight, unlike New Caledonian crows.
numbers: Eight kea. First touch: fan on 24/48 correct (50%), fan off 19/48 (40%); no effect of condition (chi2=1.775, p=0.187). Final drop was correct 47/48 and 46/48, so the birds judged weight by handling. 480 trials, 96 sessions.
limits: Small N; method adapted from the crow study. A negative in a different species, not a failure to replicate in crows.
agent_relevance: Capacity claims do not generalise across species or models. A strong result in one model may not hold in another.

source: Martin-Ordas, Call, Colmenares (2008) Tubes, tables and traps: great apes solve two functionally equivalent trap tasks but show no evidence of transfer across tasks. Anim Cogn 11:423-430
finding: The key contrast to the crows. 20 apes of four species solved a trap-tube and a trap-platform task, but success on one did not predict success on the other. No transfer.
numbers: 20 apes. Platform better than tube (F1,16=3.46, p=0.04 one-tailed). 12 solved platform, 8 solved tube; 5 solved both, 7 platform only, 3 tube only, 5 neither. Correlation between tasks r=0.13, p=0.57. Raking preferred to pushing (z=1.98, p=0.024). First trial platform 14/20 (p=0.074), tube 12/20 (p=0.37).
quote: ...apes may possess some specific causal knowledge of traps but may lack the ability to establish analogical relations
limits: Authors offer two readings: no causal knowledge, or knowledge tied to specific actions so no analogy. Species groups small.
agent_relevance: A failed transfer can come from action constraints. Our agent should check whether a failed transfer is due to the interface, not reasoning.

source: Seed, Tebbich, Emery, Clayton (2006) Investigating physical cognition in rooks. Curr Biol 16:697-701 (as reported in Taylor 2009)
finding: One rook is described in Taylor 2009 as solving a two-trap tube with transfers that reversed arbitrary cues, which suggested sensitivity to surface continuity and solidity. The crow study followed this design but changed to a tool task.
numbers: Not read directly (journal page blocked). Taylor 2009 says one rook 'may have solved' via causal relations and was not tested on a functionally equivalent task.
limits: Second-hand only. One animal.
agent_relevance: One success among many animals is an anecdote, not a capacity.

source: Visalberghi & Limongelli (1994); Povinelli (2000); Mulcahy & Call (2006); Girndt et al. (2008) as summarised in Taylor 2009
finding: Early primate work: capuchins and chimpanzees pushed food away from a non-functional inverted trap as if cues, not causes, ruled. Later work: when apes could pull, or use no tool, they did better. Taylor 2009 cites 20 of 24 apes avoiding the trap on trial 1 with a single tool.
numbers: From Taylor 2009 text only: 20 of 24 apes avoided the trap on trial 1 with a single tool (Girndt 2008). Capuchins and tamarins failed trap-table; vervets still failed 35% of trials.
limits: Second-hand through Taylor 2009; originals not opened in this session.
agent_relevance: Task format changes pass rates sharply, so a single negative probe is weak evidence of a limit.

source: Silva, Page, Silva (2005) Methodological-conceptual problems in the study of chimpanzees' folk physics (as reported in Taylor 2009 and Jelbert 2014)
finding: Adult humans also avoided the inverted trap. So the inverted control cannot cleanly tell a cue user from a reasoner, since avoiding costs nothing.
numbers: Reported in Taylor 2009 and Jelbert 2014: humans avoided inverted traps. No numbers in the second-hand text.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: A control that humans also 'fail' may be a bad control. Check controls on a known good reasoner first.

source: Farrar, Boeckle, Clayton (2020) Trialling meta-research in comparative cognition: claims and statistical inference in animal physical cognition. Anim Behav Cogn 7(3):419-444
finding: A meta-research audit of 116 physical-cognition experiments (including 14 trap-tube papers). Samples are tiny, many pass counts are low, and positive claims dominate, hinting at publication bias.
numbers: Median sample 7 animals (range 1-56). Of 87 experiments with pass counts, 15 had zero animals pass and 25 had all pass; median share passing 0.6; median 3 passers (max 17). Positive claims 44-59% depending on definition.
limits: Search was biased toward trap-tube terms. The p-value pattern is only suggestive of publication bias.
agent_relevance: Trap-tube claims rest on few animals. Treat any 'N=3 passed' story as a hypothesis.

source: Voudouris, Crosby, Beyret, Hernandez-Orallo, Shanahan, Halina, Cheke (2022) Direct human-AI comparison in the Animal-AI environment. Front Psychol 13:711821
finding: Animal-AI Testbed: children vs 30 competition AI agents on 40 tasks across ten animal-cognition levels. Children clearly ahead. Not opened this session; the Mecattaf 2024 paper (a17) reuses this child data (59 children).
numbers: Per the earlier series line (not verified here): 52 children vs 30 agents; child median 0.63 vs AI 0.35.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Benchmark design built from animal tasks is a template for our own probes.

source: Mecattaf, Slater, Voudouris, Tesic, Prunty, Cheke (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action, please: investigating the physical common-sense of LLMs in a 3D embodied environment. arXiv 2410.23242
finding: First test of LLMs on the Animal-AI Testbed (which has a causal reasoning level). Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro could do easy levels and sank on harder ones. They never exceeded the top-10 competition agents and were below children on every level.
numbers: 3 LLMs, 3 trials x 4 tasks per level (n=12 per level) against 59 children. LLMs at par with competition agents only on levels 3, 8, 9, 10 at very low rates (floor effect). An in-context 'expert example' gave no notable change; GPT level 3 rose to the upper quartile of the competition agents. Cap of 30 action scripts per episode; one 512x512 image per turn.
limits: Authors say control difficulty may dominate cognition; coarse action scripts; floor effects hide differences.
agent_relevance: Do not read an LLM's fail on an embodied physics task as a reasoning limit; the interface may be the limit. Still, an in-context example did not help.

source: Rane et al. (2025) Position: principles of animal cognition to improve LLM evaluations. ICML, PMLR 267
finding: Same logic as a trap-tube transfer. Strip the surface cues and see if GPT-4o still passes transitive inference. The pass does not hold up.
numbers: GPT-4o accuracy: A vs C 1.00; B vs D 1.00; ranked animals 0.97; random strings 0.92; reverse-ranked animals 0.78; n-term trial-based 0.40 (SD 0.50, about chance). After 60 training trials on adjacent pairs, novel non-adjacent pairs were at chance in that format.
limits: One model, one task family, prompt-format dependent. Numbers read from the full PDF, not the abstract page.
agent_relevance: LLM success that disappears when cues are stripped is the same pattern as 'avoid the hole' without the base. Add cue-stripping tests to S4.

source: Voudouris, Cheke, Schulz (2025) Bringing comparative cognition to computers. arXiv 2503.02882
finding: A short position paper. Use comparative-cognition methods to avoid both over-claiming and under-claiming in AI cognition. Names Clever Hans and tokenisation-driven arithmetic failures as the two failure types.
numbers: No new experiments. Cites that LLM arithmetic improves when tokenisation is fixed, and that image networks collapse under imperceptible changes.
limits: Opinion; no measured results.
agent_relevance: Both errors cost us: over-reading a pass (crow trap table) and under-reading a fail (apes pushing).

source: Oriental pied hornbill string-pulling study (R Soc Open Sci 2025; PMC12364582)
finding: A positive counter-example on task effects. Five of six hornbills solved two different string tasks on first contact despite foot anatomy. They used a different, fitting strategy for each problem.
numbers: Six hornbills. Mean solution time 18.13 +/- 0.25 s (secured) and 17.78 +/- 0.41 s (unsecured). Five of six solved both on the first encounter. Compare kea 9-330 s and NC crows 6-37 s.
limits: Different task (string pulling); no causal-mechanism test.
agent_relevance: Pass or fail depends on matching the task to the animal's body; the same holds for matching probes to a model's interface.

source: New Caledonian crows learn the functional properties of novel tool types (PLoS ONE 2011; PMC3237408)
finding: Crows learned that stones in a water tube raise food, and chose heavier or larger objects, but showed no benefit when the same variable was used in a search task.
numbers: Five crows. Stone number matched water level, R2=0.73. Water over sand 61% of drops (p=0.048). Heavy rubber blocks 65% (p=0.009). Search task with the same variable: 56% vs 58% in dropping, no learning. Thin vs thick tool 59% (p=0.52).
limits: Five birds, some experiments three. Individual differences large (one bird favoured sand). Read through a fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Knowledge was tied to the action context (dropping) and did not carry to search. Context-bound transfer is the pattern to expect.

source: Rooks perceive support relations similar to six-month-old babies (Proc R Soc B 2010; PMC2842627)
finding: In a looking-time test, rooks looked longer at impossible than possible support events in all four experiments. That shows expectations about support (a gravity-like rule) when no action is needed.
numbers: Mean look duration longer for impossible stimuli: Exp1 F(1,80)=8.13, p=0.006; Exp2 8.08, p=0.006; Exp3 13.64, p<0.001; Exp4 13.75, p<0.001.
limits: Looking time shows surprise, not planned use of the rule. Contrasts with action tasks where corvids fail gravity-linked probes.
agent_relevance: Competence can show in passive tests and fail in action tests. Probe format matters.

source: Founding inference model in Taylor et al. 2009: Shepard's law and triangulation (Heyes 1993; Shepard 1987)
finding: Associative generalisation falls off with perceptual distance (Shepard's law), so success on a visually distant task with the same causal structure is read as relational transfer. Triangulation uses several transfers to exclude cue accounts.
numbers: Design: initial task, 3 cue-removal transfers, 1 visually different transfer. Pass thresholds 17/20 (initial), 15/20 (transfer), 9/10 first block for early advance.
limits: Does not distinguish a shallow relation ('hole') from a deep one ('gravity'), which is exactly what transfer 3 later showed.
agent_relevance: A scoring recipe for our agent: define a pass rule, remove cues one at a time, then change the surface fully, then split proximate cue from true cause.

source: Taylor 2020 forward proposal: ratchet of hidden-object, hidden-agent, hidden-mechanism probes
finding: Taylor argues earlier tests jumped in difficulty. A fair test of 'unobservable mechanism' should be preceded by baselines for hidden objects and hidden agents in the same paradigm.
numbers: Cites the hide-stick study (Taylor, Miller 2012): crows inferred a hidden human caused stick movement; associative accounts (Boogert 2013; Dymond 2013) are disputed.
limits: Proposal only; no data in this paper.
agent_relevance: Build probe ladders with baselines so a fail points to a specific step.

source: Povinelli (2000) core thesis as quoted in Taylor 2020
finding: Povinelli's thesis: chimpanzees detect regularities between events and act on them, but do not appeal to unobservable phenomena such as force or gravity. The crow work is the first test of this in a non-ape.
numbers: Quote of Povinelli 2000 p. 298 reproduced in Taylor 2020.
quote: ...but they do not appeal to unobservable phenomena (force, gravity, etc.)
limits: The thesis is hard to falsify: any pass can be read as a proximate regularity.
agent_relevance: Warns against over-reading transfer: a pass may reflect a proximate regularity, not a general principle.

source: Low-level explanations tested in Taylor et al. 2009: chance, generalisation, hole disposition, inhibitory control
finding: The paper lists and tests low-level explanations. Chance: 10/12 first trials right but not predictive. Tactile cues: 10 of 12 first trials had no probing. Hole disposition: ruled out by non-solvers failing the table. Inhibitory control: only solvers switched sides.
numbers: Side-switching: solvers 22.1% +/- 9.0 vs 0% (U=9, p=0.0318). Espanol paused when meat reached the trap in 16.6% of trials but never switched sides.
limits: N=6. The hole-disposition test used only 3 failing crows (later 8 more).
agent_relevance: Learning to inhibit a pull may matter as much as understanding. Consider inhibition as a separate factor in agent failures.

source: Farrar et al. 2020: coded trap-tube outcomes by category
finding: The audit quotes outcomes by category. Martin-Ordas 2008 coded inconclusive; Visalberghi & Limongelli 1994 coded negative; a dog solidity study had 28 of 28 dogs fail with no learning over 50 trials.
numbers: Quoted: 28 dogs, 50 trials, no learning (Muller et al. 2014); Visalberghi & Limongelli 1994: 4 monkeys.
limits: Coding depends on authors' wording and definitions; sample is biased to trap-tube search.
agent_relevance: The same data can be coded positive or negative depending on definitions; set the pass rule before testing.
